# Overview

FastSurvival provides fast alternatives to the standard survival analysis
functions in the [survival](https://cran.r-project.org/package=survival)
package, together with a simulation layer for designing and evaluating
time-to-event trials. Every function is designed for repeated evaluation
inside large simulation loops, where the iterative or object-building
overhead of the standard implementations becomes a bottleneck. Core
computations are implemented in C++ via Rcpp.

```{r load-pkg}
library(FastSurvival)
```

# Function families

The package has two families of functions. Collett (2023) gives the
methodological background of the standard methods they implement.

The estimation and testing functions operate on a single dataset and return
an S3 object with a `print()` method. `survfit_fast()` evaluates the
Kaplan-Meier estimate at a single time point. `survdiff_fast()` computes the
log-rank test and its weighted and stratified variants. `coxph_fast()`
fits the Cox proportional hazards model for two groups. `rmst_fast()` returns the restricted mean
survival time, and `wmst_fast()` the window mean survival time over an
interval. `milestone_fast()` compares survival at a milestone timepoint, and
`medsurv_fast()` compares median survival times. `maxcombo_fast()` computes the
max-combo test, `rmw_fast()` the robust modestly-weighted log-rank test, and
`wkm_fast()` the weighted Kaplan-Meier (Pepe-Fleming) test. `ahsw_fast()`
computes the average hazard with survival weight, and `ahr_fast()` the
Kalbfleisch-Prentice average hazard ratio.

The simulation functions support a full simulation study. `simdata_fast()`
generates individual patient data for one-group, two-group, or multi-arm
trials.
`cutoff_fast()` determines the calendar time of every analysis look in every
simulated trial from combined event and calendar-time rules.
`analysis_fast()` performs interim or sequential analyses of the simulated
data at one or more looks, and can compute any of the estimation and testing
statistics above, optionally within subgroups. `switch_fast()` applies
treatment switching to the simulated data, at progression or after an interim
analysis. `pairwise_fast()` compares each experimental arm of a multi-arm
trial with a shared control. `simsummary_fast()` aggregates the operating characteristics from
the analysis output against supplied boundaries.

# A minimal example

The following example uses the `ovarian` dataset from the survival package,
with a one-sided test of treatment benefit (`side = 1`).

```{r quick, eval = requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)}
library(survival)

# Single-time-point Kaplan-Meier estimate
ord <- order(ovarian$futime)
survfit_fast(ovarian$futime[ord], ovarian$fustat[ord],
             t_eval = 500, conf.type = "log")

# Log-rank test
survdiff_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx,
              control = 1, side = 1)

# Hazard ratio from the Cox model
coxph_fast(ovarian$futime, ovarian$fustat, ovarian$rx,
           control = 1, side = 1)
```

# Formulas, data frames, and plots

For the analysis of a single data set the functions also accept a model
formula with a data frame, as the functions of the survival package do. The
control group is then the first level of the group variable, unless
`control` is given. Inside simulation loops the vector interface remains the
faster choice. Every result has an `as.data.frame()` method that returns its
estimates and tests with the same columns, and `coef()` and `confint()`
methods for the estimates; ratios are reported on the log scale.

```{r formula, eval = requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)}
fit <- coxph_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian, side = 1)
as.data.frame(fit)
exp(confint(fit))

rmst_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian, tau = 500) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

`kmcurve_fast()` builds the Kaplan-Meier curves of a data set, and its
`plot()` method can add the numbers at risk below the curves.

```{r km-plot, eval = requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
kmcurve_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, data = ovarian) |>
  plot(risk_table = TRUE, conf.style = "band")
```

# Chaining with the native pipe

The functions can be chained with the native pipe `|>` of R. A data frame
piped into an estimation or testing function is used as the data of its
formula interface. The simulation functions take the data, or the result of
the previous step, as their first argument, and `cutoff.looks` of
`analysis_fast()` and `pairwise_fast()`, like `cutoff` of `switch_fast()`,
also accepts a function of the data, so that cutoffs from a rule of
`cutoff_fast()` are computed inside the chain. Here the final analysis is at
180 events or at month 36, whichever comes first, and the nominal one-sided
levels of the two looks are only for illustration.

```{r pipe, eval = requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)}
ovarian |> coxph_fast(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ rx, side = 1) |> as.data.frame()

simdata_fast(nsim = 200, n = c(150, 150), a.time = c(0, 12),
             a.rate = 300 / 12, e.median = list(12, 18),
             d.hazard = 0.01, seed = 1) |>
  analysis_fast(control = 1, side = 1,
                cutoff.looks = function(x)
                  cutoff_fast(x, event.looks = c(120, 180),
                              max.time = c(NA, 36))) |>
  simsummary_fast(p.col = "logrank.p", alpha = c(0.003, 0.024))
```

# Where to go next

Several further vignettes cover the package in depth. *Simulation studies
with the native pipe* writes complete simulation studies as chains of the
functions above. *Validation of
FastSurvival* checks numerical agreement with established packages on a real
clinical-trial dataset. *Speed comparison* quantifies the performance gain.
*Group sequential design with the simulation trio* demonstrates
`simdata_fast()`, `analysis_fast()`, and `simsummary_fast()` against a gsDesign
reference. Further applied vignettes work the simulation functions through
nonproportional-hazards, correlated multiple-endpoint, multi-arm,
multiregional, and treatment-switching settings, and *Using your own data
generator* analyzes data generated outside the package with the same
functions.

# References

Collett, D. (2023). *Modelling Survival Data in Medical Research* (4th ed.).
Chapman and Hall/CRC.
